description: This statistical model forecasts domestic food price inflation from global indicators, with a focus on periods of macroeconomic turmoil. Patricia Toledo and Roberto Duncan of Ohio University published it in the Journal of Forecasting in 2024. The model uses dynamic model averaging, which handles both uncertainty about which predictors to include and parameters that change over time, and produces pseudo out-of-sample forecasts from a monthly dataset of about two decades for more than a hundred economies, covering the Global Financial Crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic and its aftermath. It was compared with random walk, autoregressive and time-varying parameter models. The article is available online from Wiley by subscription; its abstract is free in OpenAlex, and no code is released with it. Coverage is global. Caveats: the method is documented in the paper only, and forecasts rely on the availability of global indicator series. Dynamic model averaging tended to beat the benchmark models, especially during crises; international food price inflation was the most useful predictor for many countries in both crises, and domestic consumer price inflation and international inflation of agricultural commodities, fertilisers and other food groups gained predictive power during COVID-19. Simulation uses: a documented method for projecting food price shocks as an input to food security and supply disruption models. Related records: WFP global food prices (data-wfp-global-food-prices) and FAO food price monitoring (data-food-price-monitoring-and-analysis-fpma-p02987) provide price series for such forecasts.
